title: Emotions in Flux: How We Feel What We Know Education Underwood, Terry
author: Underwood, Terry
summary: Terry Underwood surveys four converging research perspectives -- empirical, computational, comparative, and aesthetic -- that have fundamentally rewritten the story of what emotions are and where they come from. The traditional view of emotions as fixed biological circuits (a fear center, a disgust module) has been replaced by a constructionist picture in which emotions are assembled from overlapping neural networks, shaped by culturally inherited concepts, and put to work regulating the body across time. Crucially, this regulation is not solitary: from infancy onward, human beings manage their internal states through relationships, meaning the concepts we use to name and contain our feelings are inherited from the people who first held us. The article extends this into the classroom with significant force -- a child's persistent fear of math is understood as a calibrated allostatic prediction assembled over repeated experiences of shame, not a simple cognitive error to be addressed from above. Responsive teaching, on this account, is allostatic co-regulation: a teacher reading and adjusting to the predictive states a class brings with it, often before students can articulate what they need. The article ends with a pointed distinction: what large language models structurally cannot do is connective labor -- the work of actually being changed by a student's particular reality -- which turns out to be the irreducible core of what teaching is.
points: * The brain constructs emotions from overlapping networks for affect, attention, language, and memory -- there is no discrete fear circuit or anger module -- which means that the emotion concepts a child learns from caregivers and teachers are partly constitutive of what the child actually feels, not merely labels for pre-existing states. * Emotions are the brain's long-horizon allostatic tool: where a reflex regulates the body in milliseconds, an emotion allows a person (or a classroom) to anticipate and prepare for physiological and relational needs that lie days or weeks away -- giving teachers a new vocabulary for what they are actually managing in the room. * A child's 'math fear' is best understood as a prior, not a cognitive deficiency: the body has assembled a predictive expectation of shame from accumulated experience, and no metacognitive prompt dissolves a prior -- it can only be revised through repeated, embodied experience of being met differently. * 'Connective labor' (Allison Pugh's term) -- attuning to and being actually changed by another person in real time -- is the form of teaching that LLMs structurally cannot perform, because the meeting itself is what is being delivered, not a content output. * The teacher's role reconceived through this framework is allostatic co-regulation at group scale: adjusting pace, voice, and proximity to meet the predictive states students bring before they could ask for what they need. quotes: What the brain has is a neural reference space -- a set of interacting networks for affect, attention, language, and memory that combine, recipe-like, into an interpreted experience that gets called 'fear' in one context and 'grief' in another.
To experience anger as anger requires already having the concept of anger. The word is partly what makes the experience cohere.

What is unique about humans is that this regulatory work can unfold on a long time horizon. A person can sit with an emotion, reframe it, weigh whether to act now or wait, imagine how a decision will feel a week or a decade out.

Allostatic literacy learning. That phrase is worth pausing on, because in classrooms where metacognitive has long been privileged, allostatic names something the metacognitive vocabulary cannot reach. Metacognition asks a child to manage her thinking from above. Allostatic work happens below and before that -- in the regulatory anticipations the body has already made by the time the activity starts.

A responsive teacher is doing allostatic co-regulation at the scale of a group: reading the affective anticipations a class has brought with it and adjusting their own pace, voice, and proximity to meet what the children need before they could even ask for it.
It is labor because it can't be done effortlessly, and the effort is the connection itself. It cannot be standardized, scaled, or automated, because the meeting is what is being delivered.
The classroom that shares space with LLMs is not primarily one that must defend against substitution. It is one that has to recover its own description of what it has always been doing.

A child whose math-prior needs revising needs a teacher whose presence, over weeks, gradually sustains a different prediction. A child whose journal becomes self-authorship needs peers and an adult who actually read what was written, who were changed by it in some small way, and revealed it." Page 2
